sections.heading: The Minimal Architecture | The AIM Framework
sections.content: Carried by: AIM Treatise, Chapter 4, Section 4.2.1 AIM Treatise, Chapter 4, Sections 4.3 and 4.3.6. The four primary components and the Belief Register are summarised below. The Observer row is read subject to the Minimum Installation Condition (4.3.3.1): in the social special case its output terminates asymmetrically, positive-valence installation being interminable in the M-channel until acquisition, which then re-ranks the Object-field, and negative-valence installation terminating pursuit while retaining monitoring-Salience. AIM Treatise, Chapter 4, Section 4.4.2. Appendix A AIM Treatise, Chapter 4, Sections 4.4 and 4.6.6. AIM Treatise, Chapter 4, Sections 4.2.1 and 4.4.2. The architecture and its formal results stand without Premise 9, whose default depends also on what fills the perceived field. The framework rests on a minimal architecture of four primary components and the loop that couples them, worked out mathematically. Its central results follow from that architecture, and the framework is falsifiable. The AIM Framework describes the system that produces wanting as four working parts and one store of beliefs. The Body Manager reports what the body lacks. The Observer reads what stands out around you. The Thinker holds your beliefs and works out what a want is about. The Decision Hub combines all three into one value and picks an action. The Belief Register holds what the Thinker has concluded, so the Observer can use it instantly. Combines the three signals into one value for each option and selects the action. The Decision Hub is the component whose primary function is action-selection. The Decision Hub receives valuation inputs from the other three components, integrates them into a single Common-Currency Scalar, and emits a selected action for execution. Signals when the body is short of something (food, water, warmth, rest, relief from pain) and goes quiet once the shortfall is repaired. The Body Manager is the component whose primary function is homeostatic deficit signalling and deficit-repair termination. The Body Manager produces valuation signals scaled to the deficit states of the body or body-analogous system it monitors, and terminates those signals on consumption or repair. Holds what you believe about the world and yourself, and works out explanations, including what a given want is about. The Thinker is the component whose two architecturally inseparable primary functions are, first, continuous maintenance of the priors that make assessment, recognition, and resolution possible for the whole system, and, second, Ground-Resolution, the evaluative operation that resolves whatever the Thinker is attending to into its best-supported explanation by redistributing probability mass across the Hypothesis Space, of which the resolution of the Decision Hub’s tag-stripped Scalar into a ground-attribution (an answer to what the value is grounded in) is the source-attribution special case. Continuously reads which things around you stand out as worth pursuing or avoiding, shaped by what you already believe. The Observer is the component whose primary function is continuous conditional Salience assessment over the perceived Object field, conditioned on priors maintained by the Thinker. Holds the Thinker’s current conclusions so the Observer can use them instantly. It stores; it does not compute. The Belief Register is the architectural form in which the Thinker’s current posteriors and Salience-conditioning templates are made available for downstream access at timescales shorter than the Thinker’s deliberative cycle permits. The Belief Register is not a fifth processing component, and the minimality of the specification is a claim about the components that compute, which remain four. Together the components form one loop: the Body Manager reports a deficit, the Observer marks Objects in the field, the Thinker contributes its last resolution, the Decision Hub adds the three signals into one signed value and selects an action, and where that value poses an open question the Thinker works out an explanation of it and writes the result to the Belief Register, which shapes what the Observer marks next. Remove any component and the system cannot produce the observed outputs. Remove the Observer and nothing in the surroundings, other people included, can enter valuation. Remove the Thinker and priors collapse, leaving the Observer with nothing to condition its assessment on and leaving integrated valuations with no resolver. Remove the Body Manager and deficit-repair termination is unavailable. Remove the Decision Hub and the signals cannot be integrated for action-selection. Remove the Belief Register and the Thinker’s posteriors cannot condition the Observer’s live computation, severing the slow path from the fast path. Readers with a mathematical, engineering, economic, or formal-modelling background who wish to see the operation of the architecture at each level expressed in formal terms are directed to Appendix A, which provides the formal treatment. The derivation fixed nine premises, the Construction Premises: the empirically grounded commitments from which the Minimal Architecture Specification was built, and the minimal set the construction required. With the components specified, each premise can be located in the architecture: five are carried by its components and four are derived from it. The Construction Premises are where the architecture’s construction started, not what the AIM Framework rests on. The Framework rests on the architecture (4.3 to 4.4.2), and every claim in the chapters that follow is derived from it. Human motivation arises from exactly three functionally distinct sources (Appetites, Intrinsic Motivation, and Mimetic Desire), distinguished by what each encodes and by how each terminates, and no additional source is required for a parsimonious, falsifiable account of human motivation. The Three-Source Taxonomy is the claim that motivation has three sources and no more. Appetites (A) are the signals the body sends when it departs from a set-point, such as hunger, thirst and the drive to breathe, and they end when the deficit is repaired. Intrinsic Motivation (I) is engagement that is rewarding in the doing; it deepens rather than ending, though each process it sets closes when the state it was for is reached. Mimetic Desire (M) is the reading of which Objects in the perceived field stand out as mattering, with the wanting taken up from what others are seen to want as its social special case; acquiring the Object closes no deficit, so it has no end. Cannon, W.B. (1932). The Wisdom of the Body. W.W. Norton & Co. Deci, E.L. & Ryan, R.M. (1985). Intrinsic Motivation and Self-Determination in Human Behavior. Plenum. Girard, R. (1965). Deceit, Desire, and the Novel: Self and Other in Literary Structure. Johns Hopkins University Press. (Original work published 1961) the Body Manager (4.3.1), the Thinker (4.3.2) and the Observer (4.3.3), the three components whose signals the Decision Hub integrates. Why does the AIM Framework say there are exactly three sources of motivation and not four? Is loneliness an Appetite, Intrinsic Motivation, or Mimetic Desire? The three motivational sources converge in a Common-Currency valuation that assigns each Object a single scalar subjective value, converting unlike inputs into one comparable metric, and action-selection runs on that value. The best-current localisation of the valuation is the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) and the ventral striatum. Levy, D.J. & Glimcher, P.W. (2012). The root of all value: a neural common currency for choice. Current Opinion in Neurobiology, 22(6), 1027–1038. Chib, V.S., Rangel, A., Shimojo, S. & O’Doherty, J.P. (2009). Evidence for a common representation of decision values for dissimilar goods in human ventromedial prefrontal cortex. Journal of Neuroscience, 29(39), 12315–12320. Bartra, O., McGuire, J.T. & Kable, J.W. (2013). The valuation system: A coordinate-based meta-analysis of BOLD fMRI experiments examining neural correlates of subjective value. NeuroImage, 76, 412–427. What is the Integration Equation in the AIM Framework and what do the weights mean? How does the wanting-liking dissociation support common-currency integration? After Common-Currency Integration, the source decomposition is not preserved in the output signal: the integrated value does not determine how much each source contributed to it. Downstream circuits, including those supporting conscious introspection, read the integrated value and not the inputs that produced it (Scalar-Only Delivery), and so cannot recover the decomposition from it. Source Opacity does not rest on the studies listed here. It follows from the many-to-one integration of Construction Premise 2: once three contributions are summed into one value, no reading of that value recovers the three, and introspection reads the value (Scalar-Only Delivery). Nisbett, R.E. & Wilson, T.D. (1977). Telling more than we can know: Verbal reports on mental processes. Psychological Review, 84(3), 231–259. Lebreton, M., Kawa, S., Forgeot d’Arc, B., Daunizeau, J. & Pessiglione, M. (2012). Your goal is mine: Unraveling mimetic desires in the human brain. Journal of Neuroscience, 32(21), 7146–7157. Cantor, J.R., Zillmann, D. & Bryant, J. (1975). Enhancement of experienced sexual arousal in response to erotic stimuli through misattribution of unrelated residual excitation. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 32(1), 69–75. derived from the Decision Hub’s many-to-one integration, in which three inputs yield one output (4.5.1). If introspection cannot tell me where a want came from, how can I ever find out? What is the Salience-Deficit Conflation Principle? When the Individual is moved to explain something whose cause it cannot read, its default is to settle on an explanation rather than register that none is available, and the explanation it settles on is the most plausible one among those it can form, whether or not that explanation is true. Where the thing to be explained is the Individual’s own wanting, the cause it cannot read is the source decomposition (Construction Premise 3), so every source-attribution introspection offers is constructed rather than read. Confabulation is a sincere but wrong explanation: sincere because the Individual has no introspective access to its wrongness, wrong because it fails to correspond to the state of affairs it concerns. Gazzaniga, M.S. (2000). Cerebral specialization and interhemispheric communication: Does the corpus callosum enable the human condition? Brain, 123(7), 1293–1326. Wegner, D.M. (2002). The Illusion of Conscious Will. MIT Press. Johansson, P., Hall, L., Sikström, S. & Olsson, A. (2005). Failure to detect mismatches between intention and outcome in a simple decision task. Science, 310(5745), 116–119. derived: Source Opacity combined with the Individual’s need to give an account of their own behaviour, resolved by the Thinker (4.5.2). What is the Romantic Lie and how does it relate to Confabulation? Why does challenging someone’s reasons make them more certain, not less? Mimetic Desire does not generate its own independent Object-category. Its Salience reading falls on Objects that already carry A- or I-functional roles, and integration renders that reading as additional value attached to them, a Mimetic Premium experienced as intrinsic to the Object rather than as socially added. Object Parasitism is the pattern in which the Mimetic reading of what others value is mis-attributed to a bodily deficit or an engagement opportunity, so that the acquisition it drives never meets the conditions that would end it, because no genuine deficit or opportunity was present.
